title: The Three Spots That Leak First
description: Most Houston-area leaks start at a pipe boot, a wall flashing, or a valley, not in the middle of a shingle.
html:
Homeowners point at the middle of the slope. The water almost never starts there. It starts where the roof changes: a pipe, a wall, or a valley. Those details fail years before the field shingles give up.

Pipe boots

Every plumbing vent wears a rubber or lead collar, the boot. Sun cooks the rubber until it cracks in a ring around the pipe. The crack is small. The rain that hits that pipe runs straight down it into the deck. From the attic, the stain is a circle around the pipe, often far from the wet spot on the ceiling because water travels along a rafter before it drops.

A cracked boot is a roof repair, not a new roof, unless the shingles around it are already done. We replace the boot and re-seat the shingles so the next five years of UV are not your problem.

Step flashing at a wall

Where a roof meets a sidewall, each shingle course should have its own piece of metal, the step flashing, with counterflashing or siding lapping over it. Caulk smeared along that joint is a patch, not a detail. Wind drives rain sideways in a Houston storm, and caulk shrinks. The leak shows up inside the wall, sometimes a room away, and people replace drywall twice before anyone opens the siding.

Valleys

A valley collects the water from two slopes. An open valley shows the metal. A closed valley hides it under shingles. Both fail when debris sits there, when the metal is short, or when someone wove shingles tight with no room for water. Leaves from one oak can dam a valley for a whole season. The ceiling stain lands near an inside corner of the house.

If you are chasing a stain, tell us which of these three is above it. A roof inspection that starts at the stain and walks uphill finds the source faster than a new coat of paint. Request a free inspection, or call (281) 541-0027.
